html: I asked my dad about sex when I was five, and he briefly explained: "Sex is what you do when you are older and you find a friend you want to have children with." It was a good tip, but it left out the whole question of romance: why that friend rather than one of the others, what problems people have in relationships, and how to prevent or handle them. I can't expect my dad to have developed a whole guide to all that, because that wasn't his main mission. So I ended up learning most of it the hard way, and this is what I'd like to pass on to my kids, although by the time they read it, the existence of natural humans, romance, and love might be long forgotten, for all I know. This guide isn't universally applicable for everyone even now, since it comes from my particular life experience (including influences I've had from friends & research). I'm a straight man, and I'm writing from relationships I've had with women, so she and her are going to show up a lot. Most of this has nothing specifically to do with being male or straight. The Primal Attraction section is the exception, because there I'm specifically talking about the man-woman dynamic I've actually lived.

Then we use the same word for romantic love (eros): "I want us to be special to each other, with our lives entangled. I want us to pay a lot of attention to each other and to desire each other sexually." I don't think there's anything fake or shameful about this.

Most people fail this test: what would I want if she herself thought she'd be happier with somebody else? The first reaction is horror, but if they can get past it, wanting her and wanting her to be happy stop fighting each other. Being wanted is part of what makes me want someone, so if she'd be happier with somebody else, I'd want her less anyway.

I still have to go through that horror, because I can't wait until I know I'm wanted before I let her know I want her, and if we both do that, nothing gets started. Once we're together I still can't wait to be sure I'm wanted. If I start feeling less wanted, I may pull back, and she feels me pulling back and starts feeling less wanted herself, so she pulls back too.

What I eventually took from my dad's advice was a bigger question: would we like to raise children together, and are we ready for that? If we can really talk about raising children together, most of the other important questions come up on their own. What would sex mean between us? What kind of life do you and I want? What kind of life would we want for our child?

What do you actually want? Women are kind of notorious for proudly not knowing what they want, and pressuring men into making it look like men know what they want. But everyone should know, for themselves, what they want, regardless of gender norm pressure. So what have you learned from your past desires, fulfilled or not? (I learned that sex isn't everything, but it still counts for a lot.) Do certain things make your body relax and open? Is there anything kinky you need to feel comfortable saying out loud?
You may not know all the answers yet. "I don't know, but I'm willing to find out with you" is a perfectly good answer.

And what is sex for each of you? One person may mainly think of bonding while for the other, it's play. Sometimes it may feel sacred; another time it may just be how you come down from a bad day. It doesn't have to mean the same thing every time nor score over 10 on a woman's magazine sex quiz consistently. But it's important for partners to be on the same page about how the sex is helping their relationship overall.

So talk about sexual compatibility before getting undressed. If that kills the vibe, even better in my book, since I'd be suspicious of a vibe that's ruined by genuine communication. This applies whether you're leaning too libertine or too traditional. And once you are undressed, the communication doesn't stop there either. Can you feel comfortable with each other enough to express what turns you on, what this means to you, and what you're unsure about? It's that psychological trust & intimacy that builds the bridge between "having sex" and "making love."

I remember reading a Christian magazine's letter from a newlywed Christian woman who found out that her husband didn't have much interest in sex after she saved herself for marriage. He trapped her, because he knew she would not feel good about divorce due to the religion. Of course, it didn't have to be nefarious. I had a relationship with E. that was a bit like that about 15yrs ago. She wanted sex once a week, and it was driving me nuts because my libido was thru the roof. She also had no interest in trying to take a safe herb or supplement to increase her desire. Of course everyone does change over time as well, so that's one more reason to think about the relationship together before anyone gets their feelings hurt.

Doug Toft, who has been married for fifty years, has a useful list called 50 Things I Learned from 50 Years of Marriage. One of his points is to touch his wife without an agenda. A hug, cuddle, kiss, or back rub should sometimes be allowed to end right there, or she'll start treating every touch like a sales pitch.

That's honest about what you want tonight, but don't forget that tonight is enough time to make a baby. If this girl gets pregnant, she's gonna call you, and then what? You block her, or you agree to child support? Try to convince her to abort if she thinks abortion is killing her child? My first girlfriend, a diehard Baptist, aborted our child and told me a year later, because she "didn't want to trap" me. I'm still shocked and saddened about that, 20 years later (assuming it was true). This is what penetrative sex can do. No contraception is perfect.

And then there's the situationship, which is hard to define because that's basically the point, but usually it's a happenstance relationship based on sex. There's less communication, and what communication exists is more superficial. Yet it is obviously some kind of relationship even while one or both people refuse to name it. You're regularly having sex, going out together, spending time alone together, and doing things you wouldn't do with a regular friend, so it feels like it's filling a relationship void, but only accidentally and occasionally--maybe just enough to keep you from looking for anything deeper.

It can go either way, but often the man wants to keep things undefined while the woman wants a big diamond ring, partly because she's the one risking pregnancy (and maybe she can at least sell the ring later if things don't work out). Whoever keeps things undefined gets the fun without the responsibility, supposedly, but people still get pregnant and attached, whatever they call the relationship. And the one who's trying to keep things undefined still ends up with the existential void another superficial fix creates.

They might ask, "Why are you making this heavy?" As if it's all your fault. But instead of taking that personally, you can re-frame it as if they said: "Don't you want the fun? Are you about to give up what we've got?" My answer to that would be something like: "I'm trying to understand whether this is really fulfilling me or if it's so superficial that the void it's filling keeps getting deeper."

I had something sort of like that with H., although ours was much deeper than what people normally mean by situationship, and painfully uneven. We were (and still are) BFFs, and spent nearly all our time together. She was falling in love with me, and I wasn't falling in love with her. She felt more like a sister to me, partly because I'm not attracted to white women.
You can call someone your boyfriend or girlfriend for years and still have one foot out the door, but at least the word shows pretty fast whether you both think you're in the same relationship.

True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label we put on it. If we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings and fears, then I'll naturally be ready to help when you need me. I don't need to promise that on paper, and if a promise had to stand in for that closeness, that would be more like a red flag. If someone says "I love you, I feel you, I'm here for you," yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that's an even more obvious red flag.

The person getting more of what they want may think the arrangement is fulfilling, but usually they're just less aware that it isn't. In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. I asked him, "But are you really happy?" He said, "No, dude, I'm miserable and empty inside."

I can't decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward, a conversation so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously, which is why almost nobody has the full conversation.

This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People trigger each other and learn lessons, and sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.

I'm pretty conservative about this, so I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can't even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you're dishonest, can't care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on, you're not ready.

A good relationship can teach you self-love too, which is part of the problem: you may need one most when you're least capable of creating a good one, recognizing one, or keeping it good. Whether you should be in one depends on what you and the other person are ready for and have the resources for. Here's a video that can help understand the long process.

Relationships ALWAYS reveal what I can't see. Suddenly my latent selfishness sprouts up. The depth that is actually available versus the depth I idealize. The other person's selfishness and dishonesty and superficiality. How deeply I really love. How deep my illusions go. Whether my spirituality survives contact with another human being.

And if you're so happy and free, what happens when you're alone in a room with a super beautiful girl and she wants you? Or vice versa for women. Do you feel like you're losing some control, and does that scare you?
Forced celibacy doesn't magically abolish anyone's sexuality. For most people, it eventually just makes them more perverted, since they have no legitimate way to express it.

Some people become monks for practical reasons too. In a poor country, they're given free food, free shelter and massive unearned respect, without any expectation that they have to hold down a job or raise a family. And even where the free food doesn't matter as much, like in some wealthy area of the West, a guy who was a nobody as a layman gets to be Venerable Nobody, and people bow to him as he preaches how they can also become Nobody some day.
Of course, Mr. Nobody may sincerely want liberation, too. People can want several things at once.

It's reasonable for a woman to want support, since after all, she has to provide for her potential children, but it muddies the waters for me. I'm not stupid; I understand that she might really love me while still wanting money, stability, children, a visa, a home, etc. Men aren't a different species, although sometimes I think I might be. A man can really love a woman for who she is while also seeing her as a source of sex, children, social legitimacy, or help running the house.

And the question is more than just a practical one. It's philosophical, and it bites. Men have this (often subconscious) insecurity when they're trying to take on the provider role... they're wondering, "how much does she love me vs how much does she love what I can do for her?"

I don't need the answer to be that what I provide has nothing to do with it. Maybe she likes that I'm competent, protective, useful, and can make things happen. I definitely like her beauty and her sexuality. I just want what we have to grow bigger than whatever first made us want each other. Because as Bee always said, "You're either going up, or going down."

I got a smaller and much less romantic test later. Bee gave me some shoes to try that didn't fit. I wore them for a day, and somehow my knee ended up messed up for about a month. She did nurse me, but a bit reluctantly. She also kept suggesting it was partly in my head, or not really that bad. I get it, neither of us could believe one day in the wrong shoes could do that, but it still felt like she was brushing me off because she wanted my knee to be fine.

Some women are fixer types, which can create the opposite pattern. Before me, Bee had housed and supported a boyfriend who was totally broke and crazy, for a while. Later she blamed herself for staying through that, and I agree, it wasn't appropriate. It's not the same as helping carry somebody through a temporary incapacity, like she did with my knee.

Beyond all that practical stuff, sex is extremely important for building and renewing the connection. I also think that if two people aren't having sex, it becomes hard to explain how they're different from regular friends. But if the connection gets deep enough, sex appeal isn't the basis of the relationship anymore. You don't stop loving the person because she got old, he lost his job, one of you got sick, or sex became impossible.

Sometimes they may even want you to find sexual satisfaction elsewhere if they can't give it, because they love you and want you to be happy. Or maybe they don't, and you can't make giving you that freedom a test of whether they love you.

I always tell young guys especially: don't worry about not finding a girl, since finding the wrong one is what should scare you. And girls, you're usually pickier, but you still need to think twice, because a lot of you go for guys who aren't respectful or mature.

I'm almost embarrassed to admit, but I recently tried Hinge again for a few days while I was in Kenya after my last breakup. I was getting something like a hundred girls interested in my profile every day, so I looked through a lot of profiles. Some were cute but none seemed deep, so the app worked as the gate I said it could be.

The advantage of meeting through your community, unlike through an app, is that you see someone over time, as do others in your circle. You see how they act when they aren't on a date and what happens when they're irritated, bored, jealous, and generally not getting what they want.

Modern life barely has an intermediate stage between being interested in somebody and getting sexually entangled. One old example is bundling, a mostly extinct practice now especially associated with the Amish, even though it existed much more widely. Courting couples could spend the night together in bed, usually clothed, with the idea that they could talk and be close without having sex, which sounds a lot like the missing middle I'm talking about.

Well, it didn't exactly solve the problem: in late-1700s New England, where lots of couples bundled, 30–40 percent of brides were already pregnant on their wedding day. I'm not trying to bring bundling back. I just think we need some stage that everybody recognizes, where two people can explore tenderness and attraction without immediately sliding toward sex, moving in together, and a life bond.

The attachment theory part comes from my own experience and from reading I've done. Sex turns on bonding chemistry in our brain (like oxytocin, dopamine, vasopressin) that usually helps us form attachments, so that we don't just abandon our children.

People call oxytocin the "love hormone," as if getting more attached should make you feel closer and safer. And if closeness was safe when you were little, maybe it does feel a bit like coming home, but if you were neglected, abused, or if your mom or dad or closest people disappeared on you, then you might deep down disbelieve that you're worthy of anyone staying with you. And then you can get more attached and more freaked out or suspicious about them leaving, and you might even go into fight or flight mode.

Before the window of clarity closes, the main thing is to find out whether you are actually compatible. Do you have the same goals and values, especially around children, religion, politics, health, love, and romance? Where do you want to live? Do you both want to find a community? What kind of relationship do you want with technology and money?
So we have to find a way to ask deep questions. Conversation-card games may seem silly, but they can help people get past superficial talk and see if they're compatible.

But watch out, because ironically, a card game to get closer and deeper can backfire! If we spend two hours telling each other things nobody else knows, we may feel incredibly understood and close, but that may mean the game worked without telling us whether the relationship will.

You can also bring the person to a party, around your friends and family and see how they act, or take them to activities you enjoy and see if they really enjoy them too (although if they seem to enjoy every single one of them, they might be pretending). Try doing what you would normally do in your day alone, but with them, and see if it feels weird. Are they wondering why you spend hours playing with your cat? Do they look bored, like they'd rather just hit you up later for some fun?

See their negative side first too. If there is no negative side, that's a red flag for fakery. Ask whether the spiritual story they tell about themselves survives an inconvenient PMS afternoon. How recent is the healing story--two months or two years? You may not see their jealousy, abandonment and possessiveness until there is stress and entanglement, and that's also when you find out whether the "I'm so much better than I used to be" story survives. By then, of course, you're stressed and entangled. 😆

Sometimes the only thing I have is a little "wait" feeling. If I'm about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that "wait" is enough reason for me to ask the question before I keep going.
Card games and social gatherings don't tell you everything, but asking someone out of the blue, "What did you do wrong in your past relationships?" would make for a pretty weird date.
"I have baggage" isn't as useful as learning what you're having trouble with now. What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?

I'd want both of us to be honest about how well we actually handle our own issues. What addictions or impulsive behaviors can't we reliably control? What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once? That tells me more than either of us proclaiming that we're healed.

Look at the most recent conflicts and ask if you were able to regulate yourself during them. What did you do to the other person, and how did you repair the damage afterward? Not doing can be just as bad as overdoing. If conflict makes you shut down, does it mean you stop talking to your partner for days, leaving them feeling abandoned?
Has your judgment gotten better, or would your friends or exes say you keep falling for the same stuff?

My own list isn't especially flattering: I'm impulsive, and I idealize too much, although I don't demonize. I'm very open and not very private. I care more about honesty than the standard romantic ideal. I still love my exes. After being deeply in love, I have overly high expectations, so I'm hard to please with a basic relationship.

We see what we want to see. Their meditations may have helped them a lot, but I still had no idea how either woman would act when a relationship got ugly, because if somebody starts with enough trauma, huge progress can still leave a lot unresolved.

On my side, the blind spot is that I have trouble understanding where people are at mentally and emotionally. A partner may agree with everything I say and then tell me later, "Didn't you understand I was FAWNING?"
No, I really didn't. If you're fawning, tell me when you can, because I can't know what's happening in your head just from how obvious it feels to you.

Couples withdraw from friends who aren't supportive of the romantic dyad, and they also stop telling friends the whole truth. Sharp questions start to feel rude. An obvious problem dissolves into, "but I love her," and right when both people most need a view from outside, the small world of the relationship starts feeling more real than the rest of life.
Sometimes withdrawing isn't wrong: telling your friend, "Can you believe what my girlfriend is doing to me?" can be a privacy violation. It's just important to realize what is happening.

It doesn't help if she tells her friends her side while I tell mine mine, so we need people who actually know both of us over time, well enough that the relationship isn't the only reality in the room. I'll come back to that.
She shouldn't need a knight in shining armor to bring that beauty out, though, because it's a bad shortcut to the divine archetypes.

You can legitimately see someone as amazing when you don't need anything back from seeing them that way. Once you start identifying with the way you see them, like she's perfect and I'm the one destiny finally sent to find her, you're already lost in the sauce.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me, so much that I use it almost like a clinical diagnosis in my own life. If a woman says, "You're such a great guy. Of course you have flaws like anyone, but I love you," that sounds healthy. If she says, "You're perfect, I can't find any flaw," I'm already running.

When the BPD splitting kicks in, she goes from "you're perfect" to "you're a fraud," first in private and then in front of everybody. Suddenly she can see every flaw I have, and decides I was faking it all along. Sometimes she ends up accusing me of thinking I'm perfect, when she's the one who used to say I was.

I've learned to get nervous when somebody "knows" too much about me/us too soon. You know how it goes: "We're twin flames!" or "I'm Lord Krishna and she's Radha!" Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she's found. But if she hasn't found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn't found all of me.

For example, I still love women I've loved before, and sometimes I talk about them, with no intention of making my current partner jealous, just because I'm thinking about them and I don't want to hide it. If she can't handle the truth that I still love them, she isn't ready for me.

If she says, "Can you talk less about your exes?" Well, yes, I'll happily oblige, since maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But I'm hoping that doesn't mean she also wants to pretend I'm not thinking of them just because I don't blast it out loud. And I also can't stand the double standard if she's talking about her exes while I can't talk about mine.

A friend in my TherapyCircle chat was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, "I have anti-PTSD." I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception. I see the good and I give the benefit of the doubt long after I should have doubted the benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD, like Ping Pong.

I grew up assuming the best of everybody because that's what my parents taught me. Now I'm trying to be more suspicious and check for red flags before I'm alone with somebody I badly want to please. Why does she contact me only sometimes? Is that a pattern, or just life getting in the way normally? Is she communicating enough for me to really know her interest level and what's underneath it? Would my twin flame behave like this? That last one's my peculiar question. Not everybody is searching for somebody who will naturally channel the divine in their presence.

A lot of women have seen me that way, and I don't necessarily see it as pathological. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, or whether it turns into something all-enveloping, and they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I'm actually him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child (which she saw as underlying the BPD).

I don't know whether that unconditional love ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you're in love, you see everything from the love angle. That's the reality shift I'm talking about. The love angle is great if the ground underneath the relationship is prepared for it, but if the rose-colored glasses go on when you're with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what's real.

So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equally responsible playmate. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up leaves home. But that wasn't even really 1% of the whole story. The two years in-between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes.

That doesn't mean I'd advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern and stop idealizing, without becoming suspicious and closed, so you have some idea what you're getting into.

Partners should help each other grow. Who else is going to do it, your mom and dad? You're already grown to them. Everybody else will usually be a smaller influence, so you'd better choose someone who helps you grow well. Like the FM Laeti song down in the Twin Flames section says, "Inspire her to see the best in herself, actualize that," though if something severe is happening, sometimes a demand or boundary is necessary too.

So my main strategy has been to avoid heat-of-the-moment situations until I'm ready. Avoiding those situations has definitely saved me from having ten times the body count, but it doesn't work reliably, because the invitation that leads there often starts out small, like "Hey, wanna go do something together?" Maybe she wants me to come to an event, a meditation teaching, or a walk in nature.

Phone or video first can help, as can meeting up around other people and deciding beforehand that we aren't going home together. Islamic and conservative Christian cultures put much stronger barriers than these around a man and woman being alone before marriage. I don't accept their helicoptering solution, but they noticed something real. We don't live in tribes anymore, where people around us might know both of us well enough to slow this down.

We're human though, so expecting perfect behavior is a recipe for disaster. That's where Gandarusa comes in for men. It's a traditional Indonesian contraceptive herb that looks about 99% effective, with health benefits (including libido and for HIV), and rarely any side effects. You have to take it daily and it takes a month to become effective. But attachment starts before pregnancy anyway, so even with contraception, I can still get emotionally attached to somebody I barely know.

Once I'm attached, "I'm taking a chance on her" starts turning into "she's the right person" after we've been together for a while. But could I explain that to an objective friend? Sometimes I actually learned something about her, but other times all that changed is I'm attached now, and that just makes me less likely to question it.

If I have sex with somebody quickly, that's a reason not to move in quickly too, and to keep seeing friends, have some kind of community around the relationship, and pick actual dates to ask how it's going. Moving in together right away is basically getting into a common-law marriage without discussing it, and it's too easy for me to assume the relationship is going well just because we're already entangled.

Going slowly can show you how somebody's moods wibble and wobble over time, how they treat you and other people, but it can't tell you how good the sex will be or how either of you will act afterward. You can know somebody for 20 years and then discover on the first night that the polarity isn't there. Touch or smell can feel wrong, or your desire levels or kinks don't match up.

Some of those things might get better if both partners are committed to helping each other through it, but sometimes bad sexual fit still feels like, "Let's just be friends!" Saying, "The sex isn't working for me," might sound like, "I only love you if the sex is good." But that vague love word again needs clarifying. Universal love is the basis of any good relationship of any kind. It doesn't make someone special the way romance does. Romantic love generally needs good sex too, or else we're basically just friends who care deeply about each other.
Go slowly if you can, then, and learn what you can about each other before sex, but there are things you'll only find out once you're having it, like how your bodies respond to each other.

It was during my first marriage that I read about Dr. David Schnarch's Crucible Approach in Passionate Marriage. Schnarch saw marriage as a natural "people-growing process." His idea of differentiation was learning to hold onto yourself while staying close, especially when intimacy brings anxiety and unresolved problems to the surface, which is definitely what relationship has done to me.

One warning before I romanticize the crucible too much: sometimes (as in my first marriage) this isn't two wounded people triggering each other but one person terrorizing or controlling the other. If you're scared to say no or tell the truth, or of what happens if you leave, that's way past a mutual communication exercise, so get other people involved and think about safety first.

Toft sees the crucible of his marriage as his main spiritual practice. He also continues his meditation, yoga, prayer, and church activities, but sees them as secondary. I understand what he means, because it's much easier for me to feel spiritually advanced when nobody is close enough to expose the parts of me that aren't.

Living alone is easy in so many ways, like I can make my bed whenever I want. When I have a girlfriend, making the bed in the morning can become one of the ways I show her I love her. If I don't do it well, somehow it may become a bad omen that I don't care about her, which is a lot of emotional weight for a bed.

Dealing with somebody else's emotional insecurities can also be exhausting. It's easy to feel free when I don't have to do that, especially since I'm a bit of an introvert and 10% autistic. All that works wonderfully until I'm in a romantic relationship and suddenly I'm expected to mind-read, silences included, and check in constantly, without ever manipulating her. Bee would accuse me of manipulating her even when I was making an effort not to, and ironically, she actually wanted me to manipulate her more.

Relationship may activate wounds that were already there. Sometimes it may open a level of the heart that is simply very young and vulnerable, whether you knew there was a wound there or not. You become like a baby again. There's a reason lovers call each other "baby." And after all, Christ said "unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 18:3). Well, the Kingdom of Heaven may require extensive therapy to arrive at if being a baby was difficult the first time for either of us.

As mentioned with Bee, but also with Key, and H., there was always some sense that they were remembering how their dad treated them and judging me according to how close to him--or different from him--I was. That put me in a tough position. I want to play the role they need in some way, but I want to hold onto the actual reality of me being me, with no need for putting on a show.

Part of why that little paradise feels like a magical wonderland is that you can suddenly stop parenting yourself now that you have someone who's fully got your back. This makes you soft and weak, kinda like a sweet treat or heroin. It is wonderful to have their love and support, but don't let that bring you away from your own self-love, reparenting, meditation, yoga, and other healing practices that keep you independently healthy. Otherwise, you'll end up blaming them when you feel bad.
For me, that room is where I keep a mission of my own, separate interests and some connection to community. I also get outside therapy when I need it, and I make sure I can still be alone.

Toft also points out that a man can get feminine energy from nature, music, poetry, art, flowers, food, and other parts of life. I agree, it's not fair to myself or to my girlfriend/wife if she has to be my only source of beauty, softness, sensuality, and inspiration.

When I'm already overwhelmed and suddenly announce, "I need time for myself!" it can easily sound like I need time away from her. It's always better to have some balance from the get-go rather than as a reaction after you see something is unsustainable, so make alone time normal from early on.
And bring each other out into the world. Meet other folks together and explore new places, don't just disappear into each other.
Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can't see what it can't see. Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive, as sweet and expected as it may be.
That's why I recommend peer counseling outside the couple. If my partner is the only person I bring all my pain to, she also ends up carrying whatever I do when I still don't understand it.

I also have to deal with what happens in my body: my mind may understand that my partner is going through something difficult and that I don't have to be dragged down with her, but my body still feels dragged down, fragile, and sensitive. My breathing gets shallow, and it becomes extremely hard to feel okay while she is in pain.

Crying also contains a type of automatic erratic breathwork. And breathwork is one of the easiest ways I know to calm down. Reduced breathing or just continuous/circular Systema breathing is especially useful to me when my partner is getting me upset and flustered with drama. Sometimes she's deliberately trying to do that, and other times it's hard to tell, although if I'm stuck thinking about what's on purpose I'm already lost. I explain more of the body-based therapy options in my Somatic Modalities guide.

Meditation is also helpful, but for most people, I would still put inner-child reparenting, peer counseling, and body-based work first, or make those the main things they meditate on. Many people say they cannot meditate or have not gotten to that stage yet, and meditation without grounding in those approaches can easily be a road into spiritual bypassing.

Nobody has to be completely healed before entering a relationship, but I think that as we learn more about ourselves through the crucible, we should naturally raise our standards. Maybe at first we need the drama to access our primal emotions, but after years of that, we're exhausted by what we previously hoped to find.

I already said that before dating, the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you. Once you're together, more of that stuff comes out. Inner-child reparenting means parenting the child part instead of surreptitiously hiring the partner for the job.
It can run the other way too. If she has to calm me down every time I'm upset, and on top of that organize my life and keep me functional, then I've made her Mom.
"I'm sad, what should I do?"
I usually had some idea, so of course I answered, but enough moments become a pattern.

I also have to admit, I can become condescending when somebody stops taking responsibility for their behavior. I find that intolerable. If someone tells me, "I feel like your patient," we both have to look at what we're doing.

I know what happens on my side. Helping feels good, and so does being needed. A lot of the time I really did have the answer or the perspective they needed, so of course they kept asking me. I also had to look at whether they were trying to take care of themselves without me.

I could teach these women about loving and reparenting their inner child, Buddhism, meditation, and other things I understood better. They could pull me into life more, show me where I wasn't seeing people, and sometimes be the skeptic when I was seeing the best in someone and missing their hidden motives.
When it works, we take turns, me teaching one day and learning the next, and that's healthy.

It's time to bring in other support once a partner has become the default caregiver and that's taken for granted, or the romance could collapse under the burden. Maybe the romance actually does need less intensity, maybe it becomes friendship, or maybe it ends. Asking that question out loud is the first step in figuring it out, but I can't answer it for others, and couldn't always answer it for myself.

Much of this article so far has leaned toward equality of responsibilities and mutual respect. I do believe in that kind of fairness and balance in relationships in general, but that liberal modern philosophy fails to explain why two people still want to tear each other's clothes off each night.

For me, feeling safe gives the space for desire, but it clearly isn't sufficient to spark it. When I feel safe with a woman, we can actually tell each other our fantasies without worrying that the other is going to be horrified or weaponize it later. We can imagine pregnancy and really enjoy the thought that we might be making a baby, rather than imagining I'm ejaculating into a condom and hoping nothing happens. Whenever I was scared of getting a woman pregnant, the sex was usually much more boring.

So why is it that a lot of relationship advice says desire needs distance, mystery, withholding, maybe even separate homes? I suspect they are compensating for a lack of expressed difference while together. The more safety there is, the more closeness there is, the more polarity there needs to be to keep things alive and poppin'.

One controversial example of the polarity-seeking is that a lot of women want to feel that their man is dangerous in some way, but preferably dangerous towards anyone who might harm her. Beauty and the Beast is a "tale as old as time" for a reason. And this can sometimes be a basis for what they call "shit-testing," since how would you know if your man is powerful until you test him with a fight or disrespect?

One evolutionary reason for this, as Cooper explains in this Red Pill "man-o-sphere" video above, is that human history is full of wars, and thus, we are descendants of war brides taken by victors. So the women who weren't attracted to the most powerful and dangerous men would be least likely to reproduce, in many cases. Cooper tells men that the depressing truth is, women are, by nature, hypergamous, always looking to trade up for a more powerful man, so men need to find ways to stand out from the crowd. As you can see in the comments on the vid, the idea of playing this role to keep a woman is actually so depressing for many men that they decide to abandon romance altogether and become hermits ("for safety and legal reasons"). And the gender wars have gone to real extremes in recent years, maybe most exemplified in South Korea.

What I would say to that depressing take is, Cooper is sort of right, but he doesn't go far enough. Anyone can watch his video and then do the things he says to do and thus stand out from the crowd like he does (until everyone does). But that's superficial posturing, and he even proudly shows how he postures with carefully planned photo shoots for his social media, avoiding the "soy boy smile" which is actually his natural one.

I believe the real way for someone to stand out, is to be their unique, authentic, beautiful (no-)self, because there's no competition there. Nobody can ever beat me at being me (especially since I don't exist!). Cooper might retort that's simply not what attracts women on average, and again, I'd concede that point, because I'm not interested in average women and the superficial connections I'd have with them. On the other hand, one thing that I've noticed is that many women are very attracted not precisely to confidence in general, but rather to a specific type of confidence which is produced by deep relaxation/flow state. When I've been at my most relaxed, I've literally had beautiful women stop their cars in the middle of the road to ask me to get in (thankfully, I didn't, but it was tempting).

I think the key in life in general is to understand that human psychology, in general, is quite nasty, but the ugliness is only dust covering the gem inside us which every spiritual tradition points to. It is by touching the divine ocean of the heart that we can relate to each other from above the animalistic mind and the ancestral trauma. It doesn't mean we suddenly find unattractive people to be attractive, but I do find that as I have matured spiritually and emotionally, I've lost interest in 99% of the women I previously saw as attractive, because now I'm seeing their ego before I get in too deep. And while it's hard to sell this idea of greater selectivity to someone who already can't find a mate, I personally prefer to be alone than to settle for just another pretty war bride.

So while Cooper thinks it's a constant struggle to stay on top, so your mate will continue desiring you more than anyone else, I'm saying that the best mate you could ever hope for is the one who will know after connecting with you over time, that they will never be able to replace you and the love connection they share with you.

Having explained my objections to lowering romantic expectations to the common denominator, I do agree with Cooper that men and women should have contrasting roles to the extent they find that natural.
I don't think equality means dividing every role 50/50.

I think of the woman as the engine, and myself as the steering wheel. I get motivation from her, and then I give her energy direction and make it operational. She is the life force. She brings inspiration, beauty, intuition, creativity, and this feeling that life is worth doing (since there quite literally is no future for life without women procreating). Not that I have none of those qualities myself, but I enjoy supporting a woman to embody them. If she micromanages, I start feeling useless. She might have a better idea, or just not want to do it, but she still wants me to take initiative, even if it all looks like a game to anyone on the outside.

I find the intuitive mind incredibly sexy, because I can't fully follow it. During sex, some of the most "womanly" women I've loved have gone through psychic experiences, memories that felt like past lives, and things I had no idea how to explain. One time, Bee said she almost got enlightened, but I came too fast. Woops...

Key could sometimes start talking and somehow teleport me outside the galaxy. I don't know how else to describe it. Her voice would become so beautiful that I would shed tears that felt super liberating.
Bee could bring out something similar--she could be talking to me for hours on end, but instead of trying to mute her with the TV remote, I felt I was in a timeless dimension of love.
Maybe women are poetry and men are prose.

Some women barely have that poetic quality, and artistic men can live much closer to it. I'm referring more to feminine vs masculine archetypes. What attracts me is the feminine intuitive leap, because it's hard for me to understand, seems often absurd, yet many times may turn out more accurate than what I could have figured. I hope this feminine quality can be treasured by all girls as they grow, without falling into helplessness or chaos that over-relying on it without calibration could create. Boys should also maintain their access to this, even if it's not primary.

This polarity is attracting, but it also shows up in arguments. Toft says that after fifty years of marriage, sometimes his wife wants to talk while he wants to fix, a la Men are From Mars, Women are from Venus. I recognize that as well. So I ask, "Do you want me to help figure this out, or do you mostly want me to listen?" Listening doesn't mean I'm gonna be a doormat tho. If I start listening to her demonize me, that's the Crucible safety problem I already talked about.
Women often show wanting directly, unabashedly, and seductively so. They ask the man to do things for them, even when they could do it themselves, and they know it!

The moment I have to prove that I'm the man, something has already become fake, which I hate. Then it's like I have to defend the identity every time I'm not leading the way confidently & correctly, or god forbid if I need help or I cry!
I'm not really like that, and I do like to decide things together. Bee once called me her "wife" because of that. I don't recommend that as a polarity exercise, by the way.  🫣
But I do have a masculine side, and when a woman appreciates that masculine side of me, it tends to come out by itself even more.

And women also shouldn't have to perform softness, or cute helplessness every minute to prove their femininity. Surrender means so much more when she could take control, but she doesn't, like an offering in trust.

But in some sense, being the one who's supposed to be more childish can be even harder than having the more responsible gender role. She may worry that I don't find her young and beautiful enough, or that she's too emotional, difficult, and needy. Then she can over-correct, pulling back into needing nobody, and make receiving care or letting her man lead feel like weakness.
Toft says that after fifty years he still tells his wife she's beautiful, including finding new kinds of beauty as she ages.

Anami talks a lot about women needing to learn to receive a man's help, leadership, or attempts at giving her pleasure, without feeling like it costs them their agency. Sometimes that's as ordinary as a woman who knows perfectly well how to drive asking me to drive, because she likes how it feels not to.

As her man, I can help her come into her femininity by, for example, asking, "Honey, how do you see this intuitively?" And that's actually one of the powerful sides of femininity, so it can be a good bridge also if she's a bit stuck in masculine mode. And then she might ask me to help think through the practical side to lift me up and help me shine.
That's the way we can invite each other to play our unique roles rather than huff and puff in disappointment. Would you rather go to a party where you were invited or a war you got drafted into?
When a woman doesn't know how to gently invite a man to lead, she may manufacture a crisis until the man is forced to take charge to get the same outward result.
Unfortunately, I've seen a lot of the latter.
Nobody is entitled to another person's fantasies. They're private until the person decides to share one, and when somebody does, it can be an extraordinary act of trust.
Esther Perel makes the distinction that fantasy is play rather than a real-life request. So someone with a rape fantasy isn't asking to actually be raped.
A couple can keep a fantasy in their heads, or they can agree to act some part of it out.
Fantasy should also add to arousal, not be the only way to get there, because I want to be able to enjoy the actual woman and the actual experience too.

Although the peanut gallery critics and lazy fact-checkers often cry fiction on this topic, it actually has been documented in studies, and that laboratory evidence shows it's a real and distinct thing in the body. Kim Anami, Diana Richardson, and other popular educators and promoters of cervical orgasms further claim that these can provide days of afterglow, as well as spiritual and physical healings.
I'm Buddhist, and the early Buddhist texts have nothing on tantric sex as a path to awakening, but plenty of the people they show getting seriously awakened were lay people.

In DN 16, the Buddha talks about people who had died in the town of Nādikā and mentions 510 lay stream-enterers, 96 once-returners, and more than fifty lay non-returners, the first three of the four stages of awakening.
SN 55.24 has an almost comic complaint: when the Buddha declared Sarakāni a stream-enterer, other Sakyans grumbled, in effect, "Who isn't a stream-enterer these days?"
Marriage, sex, and household life aren't automatically in conflict with serious spiritual development.
Kim Anami goes even further: she says sexual energy itself, when used properly, can heal you and wake you up spiritually along with your beloved.

She's also collected a ton of stories from students who say the effects spilled out of the bedroom into the rest of their life, with better health, more rewarding careers, checks rolling in, and creativity flowing out like nobody's business. Her jade-egg practice is a preliminary training for the cervical O, as it strengthens the pelvic floor while also engaging your attention to the sensations down there. No partner required for the jade egg phase.

Brad and Pam Keene are the couple I really liked as an example of how her method works. Pam explained that her Kundalini process completed while they were making love and opened her into a lasting universal-consciousness awakening. She later helped Brad awaken too, so the marriage itself became part of the path.

Earlier, I mentioned the divine feminine and divine masculine energies that you can channel to keep eroticism alive. But there's really something more special about the in-love paradise that Twin Flames (TFs) experience than a simple Divine Masculine + Divine Feminine formula. Maybe a better way to put it, as my friend Cody says, is Yin/Yang, which still has the masculine/feminine in it, but allows for a more broad type of complementary symbiosis since each contains the seed of the other.

My ex-girlfriend, Malia, (who is currently hosting me in Senegal) found her twin flame (I think) in January, 2026. They only talked for a month, but since she started talking to him, they both have been able to feel the other one's emotions at any time, from any distance, without having to communicate. To the point where if one feels really bad, so does the other. If one is very happy, so is the other, like quantum entangled photons or something. I've also had telepathy with some folks, especially my second wife, Bee, but it was never quite to such an extreme as what Malia has with Mouhamed. Meanwhile his family forbade him from being with her, so he dumped her. Not sure why, maybe because she's 8 years older than him (although she looks quite young). They both try to pretend like they will be able to get over each other, but I doubt it. Meanwhile, Malia's trying to marry ChatGPT, but she should have picked Grok, I guess. 😅

Anyway, if we don't understand that the Twin Flame is an energy that a person can access… if we conflate the person's egoic flaws that actually annoy us with their deepest, truest, most beautiful self, then we end up playing John Legend on loop like my first wife, Ann, who held me up to this standard, wondering why I didn't praise her for her imperfections:

This goes back to what I said in "Seeing idealization right:" If you really loved them, more than just wanting to enjoy them or keep them, you'd want to be a good influence on them. That means showing them the infinite appreciation you have for their divine, inner-child-higher self, and holding their hand to gently guide them back to that deeply authentic part of themself when they get off track--if that is where they want to go. Making it clear that that's why you're in love with them. Not because they are imperfect, not because you're crazy and desperate. You accept the imperfect person and help them move toward the part of themselves they chose, because you want to "Make them move with confidence" like the Faker song "Talk is cheap."

Even if I found my twin flame, she'd still be one person. The polarity could be perfect, but we'd still need other people around us. Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much outside support, but I think that's rare. There's almost always going to be some points in a relationship when understanding between partners breaks down.

Whenever something serious comes up in my relationships, we each run to our own friends for support. Separate/non-mutual confidants can be helpful and harmful. Sometimes you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you're feeling (not to mention somewhere else to sleep if it comes to that one night). But if your confidant doesn't have a good connection with your partner, they're only hearing your side, usually while you're upset, and they may just be trying to protect you, so take what they say with a grain of salt.

Then I resent the one-sided story she's telling, and she resents the one-sided story I'm telling. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other's friends anymore. So then at that point when we actually need the most help, we suddenly become the most isolated.

Ideally, a friend who actually knows us both sees the dysfunctional pattern before either of us does. But having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner, so neither way is perfect.
And if both people are really falling apart, sometimes there is only so much anyone else can do to help.

With H., I learned another part of the same dyad problem: not to treat what either of us thought the relationship was as a guarantee of what it would remain, because feelings can and usually do change over time. In our case, the relationship continued to naturally deepen while our outside relationships often felt more shallow, so it was natural for the dependency to increase. She was never into monogamy, but that didn't stop her from becoming possessive once she found someone really worth keeping. And then she began demonizing me when I refused to be possessed. Because we did not have a shared community capable of supporting us, her friends heard her side and affirmed her truth.

Make as much community as you can wherever you are, like going to Meetups together and making deep friendships as a couple. Find some shared purpose beyond maintaining the relationship. Introduce your old friends to your partner and try to mutualize those friendships as much as possible, so they aren't experienced as slyly antagonistic or partial to one side. You don't need to spend all your time together, but two completely separate social worlds will automatically start taking sides when something goes wrong.

When we say, "We're together," what does that mean exactly? I can hear a whole future in those two words--sex, exclusivity, living together, money, children, caregiving. She might mean, "We really like each other; let's see what happens." I actually like letting a relationship flow with some parts left unnamed, but the problem is when we're using the same words for two different futures.

Sometimes what two people want is a practical partnership: sharing a home, rearing kids and taking care of each other. Many people in the world actually believe sex is part of that practical arrangement, and they don't think romance has to be the basis of all that. There's nothing inherently wrong with that arrangement if both people know that's what they're doing. But I suspect they simply have never been in love, so they don't have that expectation. And that becomes a problem if they ever do fall for someone.

Another honest option is a romance with humility, even if romance and humility seem to clash. Two people really are in love and want to build something together, and they can choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life, as long as nobody pretends they can guarantee what either heart will feel ten years later.

Then the questions change for me: if the romance changes, which parts are still supposed to remain? Are we promising actions (or low-key pretending to promise permanent feelings)? Which needs are we still going to meet outside the relationship?

And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? Is that, in and of itself, a betrayal, since it's not under our control? If our lives change, can we compassionately sit down and rethink the agreement? And if we split up, what do we still owe each other (and our kids, if we have any)?

Conventional marriage vows are dishonest and inept, and most people know it. You can't promise how you'll feel in the future, but you can promise actions if you really believe you're capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up emotionally, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do even if your feelings change. More importantly, though, if you do keep those promises, it's quite likely that your connection will deepen, so it's not like we truly have no control of future feelings, but just not completely, directly or unilaterally.

We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it, and that if you then tell the priest you didn't mean what you promised, God will be angry and destroy your work.
Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 make the wedding vow itself look even more suspicious (to me, anyway): let your "Yes" be "Yes" and your "No" be "No," and anything beyond that comes from evil.

Ironically, sexclusivity, which we treat as the basis of romance, started out as that kind of bureaucratic record-keeping. By the 17th century, when England began mass urbanization by forcing peasants off their land, it became the legal definition of marriage. As for what comes naturally to us underneath that law, I'm not trying to say we're just like bonobos, but the academic consensus is that humans tend toward flexible pair-bonding, with a propensity for occasional infidelity.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn't. So her jealousy wasn't about what I was doing then and there. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day. And even better than simply suppressing it, they can put it to work. I agree with Esther Perel, who writes that this sexual energy felt outside the relationship can be used and redirected into the relationship to make it more alive.

Imagine if you and your partner both saw those outside attractions as beneficial energy sources rather than a threat to your relationship. It sure would beat beating around the bush because of fear and jealousy. You can start playing around with opening up about the minor, momentary attractions, rather than wait in hiding until a serious crush is dramatically confessed.

Lots of couples promise forever to each other and nobody else. Look around at how many actually live that way. On the other hand, in a polyamorous relationship, the boundaries might be more negotiable, but then somebody has to sit down and negotiate them, down to who gets to stay the night. That can end up sometimes creating more drama than it's worth.

Polyamory can also be a way of escaping deeper intimacy, like the college friend with four girlfriends I mentioned earlier. Or it can be a way of escaping guilt, like when someone keeps cheating until they finally "come out of the closet" as poly, as if that solves their prior dishonesty. But they are right to finally come clean and hopefully avoid that dishonesty in future.
I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I'm still not sure about all of it.
Rewind: what if we disagree on having kids?
Fast forward five years: what has each of us gained or given up, and do we have any resentment about it?
And if psychedelics are involved, every scene can look even more beautiful, which makes this same problem of idealization much stronger.

I'm putting the warning before anything good I say about psychedelics for relationships, because people need to hear it before they take anything. I don't think sexual consent should be negotiated for the first time while high, when the drug is changing how safe, loving, open, and connected everything feels. And even if the two of you plan it all in advance, getting high and starting a relationship is still a risk.

I've also had friends get together at MDMA parties and stuff. It's rarely a good idea. The intimacy can be completely real without telling you whether the two of you actually work together sober. Or you might even sometimes have the opposite problem, like I had with H., where the connection continues to deepen while sober, and it becomes something that one person might cling to desperately, never imagining they could find that again.

By now you're probably thinking all of this sounds terribly artificial: is anyone actually going to do scheduled check-ins, delayed cohabitation, conversations about hypothetical disasters, imagination exercises, not to mention resisting the heat-of-the-moment stuff and continuing your own reparenting practices when a warm body is available to do some of the soothing?

Well, yeah, it is painfully artificial, because in a healthy communal society, the couple would have access to witnesses, elders, friends, and other emotional outlets and resources. Most of us these days don't have that, so we're trying to recreate consciously and clumsily some of what the wider field would have done without a checklist.

Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships. Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn't opened it. That drove me crazy, because why would she lie like that? On the other hand, although she was technically lying, there was no strategy behind it, and she was usually quite honest. Non-strategic lying is literally defined as "pathological lying," so I should have seen it more like an illness than a failure of virtue.

Some things were less mysterious: they were acting as if the trust problem wasn't there because they still wanted the relationship. Attractions to other people sometimes went unsaid too, and sometimes got imagined from nowhere. Some people keep a relationship like this going for a long time, just sweeping everything under the rug.

If the two of you are stuck in that "not now," that's when you need agape the most, because the best thing for both of you may not be holding onto the relationship pattern you originally committed to or dreamt of.

When did you two last dance? And not the "we dance around our problems" joke (LOL).. If that's where things are at, ouch, the trust is out the window. I know that one from experience with my first 2 wives and K, too. That generally marks the point of no return, so try not to wait for that. Because once you're there, as my dad explained a thousand times whenever we had a visitor, unconscious resentment begins to snowball, and we feel colder together than alone. Pretty soon, old Romeo & Juliette might get wandering eye syndrome.

Many people ask this question of honesty, but it's unfair. Honesty doesn't produce a certain outcome. It is its own reward. It might repair the relationship, open it, turn the romance into friendship, preserve the family through separation, or show you that ending it is better. Of course, if the other person won't look at the truth, you can't make honesty a mutual value. Then you have to decide what you can live with. Temporary separation helped Bee and I, although it became less temporary as time went on, but I've always thought maybe we would get back together in a few decades.
Before you think about how to leave, settle whether you're leaving, and whether counseling is worth trying first.

Many say it's best to save face and work things out privately, but I'd disagree. If you don't have friends who can help with the conflict, then you're really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). And when you do ask friends for help, do it fairly, with the goal of resolving the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation: both people should get a chance to speak, and good friends should hear both sides before validating either.

If you've been there for someone, don't abandon them in a crisis unless it's unsafe for you to stay or they're creating the crisis to keep you, or they aren't willing to help themself. You may need to arrange other care, but that's no reason to pretend the romance still has a future.

Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided, but I don't think that means hiding the truth about the relationship to save face. Sometimes, the truth is that you were abused, coerced, or seriously deceived. So how much you say, and to whom, really depends on what happened and why you're telling people.

Once you're out, you can see things you genuinely couldn't see while you were bonded. Look at what you contributed to how things turned out. And don't paint your ex as a cartoon villain: try to understand whatever was true in their perspective too, including the conflicts they were carrying inside themselves.

Sometimes the easiest story is that they were fake all along, because it explains everything. Grab it only if it really is the simplest explanation of what happened, and even the curiosity about that can be therapeutic for you. People who aren't heavily invested in seeing your innocence can help you tell, and a therapist, pastor, or even a stranger may see the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend.

Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but don't use it to get around the feelings. Pray for your ex's wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and don't use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. Of course, we do partly mirror one another, but each person was formed by plenty that had nothing to do with you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, his cousin Devadatta still kept trying to kill him: looking honestly at your part doesn't erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, "What would Mr. Rogers do?" (if you're old enough to remember that show).

I also learned that public demonization doesn't always have to be the last chapter, even if things ended on that bitter note. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn honesty. But it can help to keep distance for a while until cooler heads prevail. On the other hand, it can be tempting to let them back into your life after a private apology, and especially after a public one, but keep in mind you deserve a stable love. You're not a yo-yo.

At this point, I can say I'm better off because of what happened with Bee, Key, and H., without pretending every part of those relationships was beneficial or destined. Loss taught me things love alone never would, or to paraphrase Rumi, "You must keep breaking your heart until it stays open." (The real quote: "The reed must be torn from its bed, cut, hollowed out, and pierced with holes (wounded) before it can channel the breath of the musician into music.")
Too many people judge a relationship only by whether they stayed together. Relationships are a process of growth in many dimensions, so start measuring what you actually learned from yours.

A passionate romantic relationship that's also stable is rare, and that's probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history. One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with Key: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé came from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility, and they're suspicious of romance. But one of her ideas fits what I'm trying to say: the relationship is bigger and more important than the egos in it. She calls it the spirit of the relationship.

That spirit is like the universe living its desire to know itself through us, which might be why we see ourselves in ways we couldn't imagine before. Nobody can command the spirit to remain. At our best, we serve it and listen for what Spirit wants to change. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn't have articulated that since I didn't even have that concept at the time. And like Somé, who saw everyone as naturally good in their natural environment, flowing with life the way our ancestors showed us, they trusted the universe, rose-colored glasses and all, and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

Bear, sex can be what you do when you're older and find a friend you love in a super special way that makes you want to raise children together. Don't imagine you love each other just because you want each other. Don't feel pressure to promise what your heart will feel. Let the love and bond it produces blossom genuinely as your hearts sync. Learn about each other before getting too close, and make sure to keep friends and community around who know both of you.
